title_en: NATURE REPUBLIC Co., Ltd. v. Wangdu County Jianglin Cosmetics Store — dispute over infringement of trademark rights
ruling_gist_en: In trademark infringement cases, the establishment of the alleged infringer's defense of legal source should satisfy both subjective and objective elements. The objective element is that the alleged infringing goods were legally obtained by the seller. The subjective element is that the seller did not know or should not have known that the alleged infringing goods constituted infringement. The subjective and objective elements are interrelated and inseparable, and the proof of the objective element has a presumptive effect on the subjective element.

full_text_en:
NATURE REPUBLIC CO., LTD. v. Wangdu County Jianglin Cosmetics Shop  
— dispute over trademark infringement  

【Ruling Gist】  

In trademark infringement cases, the establishment of a defendant's defense of lawful source shall satisfy both subjective and objective elements. The objective element requires that the accused infringing goods were legally obtained by the seller; the subjective element requires that the seller did not know or should not have known that the accused infringing goods constituted infringement. The subjective and objective elements are interrelated and inseparable, and the evidence for the objective element has a presumptive effect on the subjective element.  

When examining the aforesaid subjective and objective elements, a people's court shall comprehensively consider factors such as the market position of the seller, the cost of rights enforcement by the right holder, and market transaction practices, and shall set reasonable requirements for the seller's burden of proof. Evidence such as the seller's scale of business, level of professionalism, and market transaction practices may serve as evidence for determining the seller's duty of reasonable care. If the evidence of lawful source provided by the seller is commensurate with its duty of care, it may be presumed that the seller subjectively did not know that the goods it sold were infringing.  

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court  

(2022) Zui Gao Fa Min Zai No. 275  

Reapplying Applicant (Defendant at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Wangdu County Jianglin Cosmetics Shop. Domicile: New Century Commercial Street, Wangdu County, Baoding City, Hebei Province, People's Republic of China.  

Operator: Zhang Jiangchao, female, born June 15, 1980, Han Chinese, residing in Wangdu County, Baoding City, Hebei Province, People's Republic of China.  

Authorized Agent Ad Litem: Zhao Yu, attorney at Shanghai Shenhao (Tianjin) Law Firm.  

Authorized Agent Ad Litem: Zhao Lijun, attorney at Shanghai Shenhao (Tianjin) Law Firm.  

Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): NATURE REPUBLIC CO., LTD. Domicile: 24th Floor, Glass Tower, 946-1, Daechi-dong, Gangnam-gu, Seoul, Republic of Korea.  

Legal Representative: JUNG WOON HO, Representative Director of the company.  

Authorized Agent Ad Litem: Li Hang, attorney at Hebei Hangyue Law Firm.  

Authorized Agent Ad Litem: Shi Han, attorney at Hebei Hangyue Law Firm.  

The reapplying applicant, Wangdu County Jianglin Cosmetics Shop (hereinafter referred to as Jianglin Shop), filed an application for retrial with this Court, contesting the civil judgment (2021) Ji Zhi Min Zhong No. 26 rendered by the Hebei High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as the court of second instance) in the case of a dispute over trademark infringement with the respondent, NATURE REPUBLIC CO., LTD. (hereinafter referred to as NATURE REPUBLIC). This Court, by civil ruling (2021) Zui Gao Fa Min Shen No. 6332 dated June 24, 2022, decided to bring the case up for retrial. After bringing up the case, this Court formed a collegial panel according to law and held a public hearing. The authorized agents ad litem of the reapplying applicant Jianglin Shop, Zhao Yu and Zhao Lijun, and the authorized agent ad litem of the respondent NATURE REPUBLIC, Shi Han, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. This case is now concluded.  

Jianglin Shop applied for retrial, alleging:  

1. The evidence submitted by Jianglin Shop can prove that the accused infringing goods had a lawful source and that it had exercised reasonable care in the process of purchasing the accused infringing goods, conforming to the relevant provisions of laws, regulations, and judicial interpretations on lawful source, and therefore should not bear liability for damages. The court of second instance imposed an excessively high standard of care on Jianglin Shop, misallocated the burden of proof as to whether the subjective element was in good faith or bad faith, and ultimately found that Jianglin Shop's defense of lawful source could not be established, which was an error in both fact-finding and application of law.  

2. The court of second instance failed to add Tianjin Zhongzhuang Supply Chain Management Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhongzhuang Company), Tianjin Guanmei Trading Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Guanmei Company), and Qingdao Yipinzhuang International Trade Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yipinzhuang Company) as defendants, resulting in incomplete factual findings and affecting the parties' right to redress.  

3. Jianglin Shop appealed against the first-instance judgment's finding regarding the identity between the evidence it submitted and the accused infringing goods purchased by notarization. The court of second instance did not adjudicate this issue but instead dismissed the appeal on the ground that Jianglin Shop had "failed to exercise reasonable care," thus depriving Jianglin Shop of the opportunity to respond to the fact of "failure to exercise reasonable care," and damaging Jianglin Shop's procedural right to relief through the second instance.  

4. NATURE REPUBLIC abandoned pursuing the source infringers and initiated thousands of trademark infringement lawsuits against end outlets, forcing outlets to pay damages ranging from several thousand to tens of thousands of yuan, and profiting tens of millions of yuan. This constitutes improper rights enforcement, inconsistent with the judicial spirit of "enforcing rights against the source, pursuing the manufacturer," and should be regulated.  

In summary, Jianglin Shop applied to this Court for retrial pursuant to Items (2) and (6) of Article 200 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (as amended in 2017), requesting: (1) to set aside the judgment of the second instance; (2) to set aside the judgment of the first instance; (3) to amend the judgment to dismiss all of NATURE REPUBLIC's claims; (4) to have NATURE REPUBLIC bear the litigation costs.  

NATURE REPUBLIC argued in defense:  

1. The court of second instance correctly found that Jianglin Shop had not exercised due care and that the cosmetics sold had no lawful source;  
2. Zhongzhuang Company, Guanmei Company, and Yipinzhuang Company were not necessary parties to this case, and the court of second instance committed no error in failing to add them.  

Therefore, NATURE REPUBLIC requested that Jianglin Shop's retrial request be dismissed.  

NATURE REPUBLIC filed an action with the Baoding Intermediate People's Court of Hebei Province (hereinafter referred to as the court of first instance), requesting:  

1. an order that Jianglin Shop immediately cease its acts of infringing the exclusive right to use Trademark No. 10494197 "NATURE REPUBLIC" and Trademark No. 9481384 "纳益其尔" (hereinafter referred to as the involved trademarks), namely, cease producing, using, offering for sale, or selling products that infringe the exclusive right to use the involved trademarks, and destroy the infringing products in stock;  
2. an order that Jianglin Shop compensate NATURE REPUBLIC for economic losses of RMB 30,000;  
3. an order that Jianglin Shop pay reasonable expenses totaling RMB 10,000 (RMB 2,000 for investigation and evidence collection service fees, notarization fees, travel expenses, etc., and RMB 8,000 for attorney fees);  
4. an order that Jianglin Shop bear the litigation costs of the case.  

The court of first instance found the following facts:  

NATURE REPUBLIC is a legal person registered in the Republic of Korea. It owns the registered trademark No. 10494197 "NATURE REPUBLIC," with a validity period from May 7, 2013, to May 6, 2023, and the approved goods (Class 3) include perfumes, cosmetic lotions, cosmetics, etc. The registered trademark No. 9481384 "纳益其尔" is owned by a third party, Beijing NATURE REPUBLIC International Trade Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Beijing NATURE REPUBLIC), with a validity period from June 7, 2012, to June 6, 2022. On January 1, 2018, Beijing NATURE REPUBLIC and NATURE REPUBLIC entered into an "Exclusive Trademark License Contract," granting NATURE REPUBLIC the exclusive right to use the registered trademark No. 9481384 "纳益其尔" within the administrative region of the People's Republic of China for the period from January 1, 2018, to June 5, 2022.  

On January 1, 2019, NATURE REPUBLIC and the third party Beijing NATURE REPUBLIC executed a "Power of Attorney," authorizing Beijing NATURE REPUBLIC to investigate and collect evidence and preserve evidence by notarization regarding trademark infringement within the mainland of the People's Republic of China on behalf of NATURE REPUBLIC. On January 1, 2019, Beijing NATURE REPUBLIC and Beijing Hanhuiming Intellectual Property Agency Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Hanhuiming Company) executed a "Power of Attorney," sub-delegating the matters entrusted by NATURE REPUBLIC to Hanhuiming Company. On September 4, 2019, NATURE REPUBLIC and Attorney Yang Weihua of Beijing Shengqi Law Firm executed a "Power of Attorney," authorizing Attorney Yang Weihua as a specially authorized litigation agent to enforce rights against trademark infringement within the mainland of the People's Republic of China. On July 30, 2019, Zhang Shuojia A, head of the Hebei Branch of Hanhuiming Company, went to "Duoning Jianglin Daily Chemical 1 Store" on Zhonghua East Road, Wangdu County, Baoding City, Hebei Province, and purchased one box of goods bearing the "NATURE REPUBLIC" mark by swiping a credit card. "Jianglin Daily Chemical 1 Store Pedestrian Street Store" issued a shopping receipt. The purchase process was notarized and evidence was preserved by the Guoxin Notary Public Office of Shijiazhuang, Hebei Province. Beijing NATURE REPUBLIC issued a "Certificate of Identification," determining that the accused infringing goods were counterfeit products bearing the registered trademark of NATURE REPUBLIC.  

The court of first instance ruled:  

1. Jianglin Shop shall immediately cease its acts of infringing the exclusive right to use the trademarks, i.e., cease selling products that infringe the exclusive right to use the involved trademarks, and destroy the infringing products in stock;  
2. Jianglin Shop shall compensate NATURE REPUBLIC for reasonable expenses incurred in enforcing its rights and economic losses totaling RMB 10,000, to be fulfilled within ten days from the date the judgment becomes legally effective;  
3. NATURE REPUBLIC's other claims are dismissed. The case acceptance fee of RMB 800 shall be borne by NATURE REPUBLIC in the amount of RMB 600 and by Jianglin Shop in the amount of RMB 200.  

Jianglin Shop, dissatisfied with the judgment of the first instance, appealed, requesting:  

1. to set aside the judgment of the first instance;  
2. to amend the judgment to dismiss all of NATURE REPUBLIC's claims in the first instance and to have NATURE REPUBLIC bear the litigation costs of both the first and second instances.  

Its main reasons were: The evidence submitted by Jianglin Shop could prove that the accused infringing goods it sold originated from Zhongzhuang Company, and Zhongzhuang Company's products came from Yipinzhuang Company; Jianglin Shop had exercised reasonable care, and pursuant to Article 64 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Law), it should not bear liability for damages. The notarial certificate (2019) Ji Shi Guo Zheng Min Zi No. 5480 issued by the Guoxin Notary Public Office of Shijiazhuang, Hebei Province, could not be used as evidence in this case.  

The court of second instance confirmed the facts found by the court of first instance.  

The court of second instance held that the issues in dispute in this case were:  

(1) Whether the notarial certificate (2019) Ji Shi Guo Zheng Min Zi No. 5480 issued by the Guoxin Notary Public Office of Shijiazhuang, Hebei Province, could be used as evidence in this case;  
(2) Whether the source of the accused infringing goods sold by Jianglin Shop was lawful;  
(3) How Jianglin Shop should bear legal liability.  

Regarding the first issue.  

Pursuant to Article 36 of the Notarization Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 93 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, in the absence of contrary evidence from Jianglin Shop, the notarial certificate submitted by NATURE REPUBLIC to the court of first instance was admitted by the court of second instance and used as the basis for deciding the case. As to Jianglin Shop's argument on appeal that the notarial certificate (2019) Ji Shi Guo Zheng Min Zi No. 5480 was a cross-regional notarization and could not be used as evidence of infringement, the court of second instance held that the territorial notarization requirement in the relevant regulations is intended to strengthen the management of notarization and ensure orderly notarial work, and does not constitute a mandatory requirement for notarial procedures; it does not affect the authenticity and validity of the notarial certificate in this case.  

Regarding the second issue.  

Article 64, Paragraph 2 of the Trademark Law provides: "A seller who does not know that the goods it sells are goods that infringe the exclusive right to use a registered trademark, and who can prove that the goods were legally obtained by it and who names the supplier, shall not bear liability for damages." For Jianglin Shop to prove that the goods it sold had a lawful source and to be exempt from liability for damages, it must first prove that it was without fault. Cosmetics are special goods. The "Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Cosmetics" and the "Regulations on the Hygienic Supervision of Cosmetics" contain special provisions on the import, quarantine, and inspection of cosmetics. As a cosmetics operator, Jianglin Shop has a higher duty of care compared to ordinary goods sellers, and should verify the qualifications of upstream merchants and provide relevant evidence. Although Jianglin Shop provided copies of the "Qingdao Special VAT Invoice," "Tianjin Special VAT Invoice," "Inspection Report," "Yantai Customs Import Duty Special Payment Book," "Customs Import Goods Declaration Form of the People's Republic of China," and "Certificate of Inspection and Quarantine for Entry Goods of the People's Republic of China" in the first instance, NATURE REPUBLIC did not admit the authenticity of the above evidence. According to Article 11 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Procedures: "A party providing evidence to a people's court shall provide the original or the physical object. If it is necessary for the party to keep the original or physical object itself, or if it is genuinely difficult to provide the original or physical object, a duplicate or reproduction that has been verified as correct by the people's court may be provided." The above documents provided by Jianglin Shop could not prove that the goods from its upstream merchants originated from NATURE REPUBLIC, nor could they prove that they had authorization from NATURE REPUBLIC, and thus could not achieve the purpose of proof. Since Jianglin Shop failed to provide evidence to prove that it had exercised the corresponding duty of care, it must bear the adverse consequences and cannot be exempted from liability for damages.  

Regarding the third issue.  

Pursuant to Article 63 of the Trademark Law, there is no evidence in this case to prove the losses suffered by NATURE REPUBLIC due to the infringement or the profits gained by Jianglin Shop. The court of first instance's application of statutory damages had a legal basis. The court of first instance comprehensively considered factors such as Jianglin Shop's degree of subjective fault and the brand influence of NATURE REPUBLIC, and discretionarily determined the amount of compensation, including reasonable expenses incurred in stopping the infringing act, to be RMB 10,000, which was appropriate.  

In summary, pursuant to Item (1) of Article 170 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (as amended in 2017), the court of second instance ruled: the appeal is dismissed and the original judgment is affirmed. The second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 50 shall be borne by Jianglin Shop.  

The facts found by the courts of first and second instance are substantially true, and this Court confirms them.  

This Court additionally finds:  

The involved trademark No. 10494197 "NATURE REPUBLIC" on which NATURE REPUBLIC bases its claim, upon renewal, has a term from May 7, 2023, to May 6, 2033. The involved trademark No. 9481384 "纳益其尔," upon renewal, has a term from June 7, 2022, to June 6, 2032.  

It is further found:  

In the first instance, Jianglin Shop provided the product distribution contract signed with its upstream merchant Zhongzhuang Company, a copy of Zhongzhuang Company's business license, and a delivery order issued by Zhongzhuang Company. In the second instance, Jianglin Shop additionally provided its warehouse receipt and payment vouchers for payments made by Jianglin Shop to Zhongzhuang Company, which were submitted together with the first-instance evidence to prove that the accused infringing goods it sold were legally obtained. The above evidence was all originals. In addition, Jianglin Shop also provided copies of evidence relating to Zhongzhuang Company's procurement of NATURE REPUBLIC aloe vera gel products from its upstream merchant Guanmei Company, and Guanmei Company's procurement from its upstream merchant Yipinzhuang Company, including invoices, customs import goods declaration forms, certificates of inspection and quarantine for entry goods, and customs import duty payment books, to prove that it had legally obtained the accused infringing goods and exercised the corresponding duty of care.  

NATURE REPUBLIC expressed no objection to the authenticity and legality of the transactions between Jianglin Shop and Zhongzhuang Company and the related evidence, but argued that the goods involved in the above evidence could not be individually matched to the accused infringing goods and could not achieve the purpose of proof.  

At the retrial hearing before this Court, Zhongzhuang Company explicitly acknowledged that the accused infringing goods sold by Jianglin Shop originated from Zhongzhuang Company.  

Since the supplier Zhongzhuang Company confirmed the supply fact for the evidence for which originals were provided, and NATURE REPUBLIC expressed no objection to the authenticity of the transactions, this Court confirms their authenticity. The probative force of this evidence and the other evidence for which only copies were provided will be analyzed and evaluated below in conjunction with the facts of the case.  

In this retrial, this Court holds that the issues in dispute in this case are:  

(1) Whether Jianglin Shop's defense of lawful source can be established and whether it should bear liability for damages;  
(2) Whether the court of second instance's failure to add relevant parties to participate in the proceedings and its adjudication of the relevant substantive issues constituted a violation of procedural rules and damage to the parties' rights.  

(1) On whether Jianglin Shop's defense of lawful source can be established and whether it should bear liability for damages  

Article 64, Paragraph 2 of the Trademark Law provides: "A seller who does not know that the goods it sells are goods that infringe the exclusive right to use a registered trademark, and who can prove that the goods were legally obtained by it and who names the supplier, shall not bear liability for damages." Article 4 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Intellectual Property Civil Litigation provides: "Where a defendant asserts a defense of lawful source in accordance with law, it shall bear the burden of proving that the accused infringing product or reproduction was legally obtained, including the lawful channels of purchase, a reasonable price, and the direct supplier, among others. If the evidence of the source of the accused infringing product or reproduction provided by the defendant is commensurate with its duty of reasonable care, it may be found that the defendant has completed the burden of proof as referred to in the preceding paragraph, and it may be presumed that the defendant did not know that the accused infringing product or reproduction infringed intellectual property rights. The defendant's scale of business, level of professionalism, and market transaction practices may serve as evidence for determining its duty of reasonable care."  

According to the above legal and judicial interpretation provisions, the establishment of a defense of lawful source requires the simultaneous satisfaction of both subjective and objective elements: the objective element requires that the accused infringing goods were legally obtained by the seller; the subjective element requires that the seller was not at fault. The subjective and objective elements are interrelated and inseparable, and the evidence for the objective element has a presumptive effect on the subjective element.  

1. On the review of the objective element in this case.  
This Court holds that in reviewing the objective element of a defense of lawful source, one should start from the purpose of the design of this system, comprehensively consider factors such as the market position of the seller, the cost of rights enforcement by the right holder, and market transaction practices, and set reasonable requirements for the seller's burden of proof. The relevant provisions of administrative regulations may also serve as a reference for determining whether the objective element is established. Article 79 of the Implementing Regulations of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China provides that the following circumstances are among the circumstances "where the seller can prove that the goods were legally obtained by it" as referred to in Article 64, Paragraph 2 of the Trademark Law: "a supply list and payment receipt legally signed and sealed by the supplier, and the facts have been verified or confirmed by the supplier"; "a purchase contract signed by both the supplier and the buyer, and the contract has been verified to have been actually performed"; "a valid purchase invoice, and the matters recorded on the invoice correspond to the goods involved." In this case, Jianglin Shop, the seller of the accused infringing goods, is an individual retail shop, which occupies a weaker position in market transactions and typically uses more flexible transaction methods. The burden of proof on it to prove lawful source should be appropriately relaxed, without being too stringent on the completeness of the form of evidence. As long as the evidence it provides is consistent with general transaction practices, can identify the true identity information of the supplier of the accused infringing goods, and show that the accused infringing goods were purchased through lawful channels and at a reasonable price, it should be found that the accused infringing goods it sold have a lawful source.

After review, the evidence submitted by the Jianglin Cosmetics Store, including the product distribution contract and a copy of the business license of Zhongzhuang Company, showed that the business scope of Zhongzhuang Company included the sale of cosmetics, and that a purchase and sale contract relationship existed between the Jianglin Cosmetics Store and Zhongzhuang Company regarding the Nayi Qier Aloe Vera Gel product. According to the contract, Zhongzhuang Company was to supply the Nayi Qier Aloe Vera Gel product to the Jianglin Cosmetics Store, and the Jianglin Cosmetics Store was to pay the purchase price to Zhongzhuang Company. The delivery notes, warehouse receipt notes, payment vouchers, and other evidence showed that the Jianglin Cosmetics Store purchased 360 boxes of Nayi Qier Aloe Vera Gel from Zhongzhuang Company at a unit price of RMB 16, and had paid the relevant amount to Zhongzhuang Company. The product names, quantities, transaction times, and transaction amounts in the above evidence corresponded with the contract, evidencing that the contract had been genuinely performed. In addition, both the delivery note issued by Zhongzhuang Company and the warehouse receipt of the Jianglin Cosmetics Store indicated that the barcode of the Nayi Qier Aloe Vera Gel was 8806173420377, and the delivery note also recorded the production batch number and expiration date. Upon comparison, this information was completely consistent with the barcode, batch number, and expiration date printed on the outer packaging of the accused infringing product. Therefore, the evidence provided by the Jianglin Cosmetics Store showed a complete transaction chain, a lawful transaction channel, a transaction method consistent with general trading customs, and identified the supplier of the accused infringing product as Zhongzhuang Company. That is, the evidence adduced by the Jianglin Cosmetics Store has basically met the standards and requirements of laws, regulations, and judicial interpretations regarding the burden of proof for the objective element of the legal source defense, and can prove that the Jianglin Cosmetics Store obtained the accused infringing product lawfully. Given that Nayi Qier did not provide contrary evidence to rebut this, and Zhongzhuang Company also acknowledged that the accused infringing product sold by the Jianglin Cosmetics Store originated from Zhongzhuang Company, this Court accepts the above evidence submitted by the Jianglin Cosmetics Store.

2. Review of the subjective element in this case. The establishment of the subjective element of the legal source defense requires that the seller had no fault, i.e., it actually did not know and should not have known that the product it sold was infringing. According to the provisions of the above judicial interpretation, the determination of the seller's subjective state should start from examining the evidence of the legal source of the accused infringing product, and be comprehensively judged in light of the specific case facts and trading customs. The seller's business scale, degree of professionalism, and market trading customs can serve as evidence for determining its reasonable duty of care. Typically, a small-scale retailer and a business entity with a certain scale have different cognitive abilities regarding whether the accused infringing product is infringing. If the legal source evidence provided by the seller is commensurate with its degree of duty of care, it can be presumed that the seller subjectively did not know that the product it sold was infringing.

In this case, the accused infringing product, Nayi Qier Aloe Vera Gel, is an affordable daily-use cosmetic with relatively low market price and product profit. The seller, the Jianglin Cosmetics Store, is an individual industrial and commercial household with a small business scale and low level of professionalism. Therefore, its cognitive ability regarding whether the product it sold was infringing should not be required to be too high. From the evidence provided by the Jianglin Cosmetics Store, the evidence it adduced can prove that it obtained the accused infringing product in compliance with lawful and normal market transaction rules. The source of the product is clear, the channel is lawful, the price is reasonable, and it also identified the provider of the accused infringing product as Zhongzhuang Company. This should be considered as having fulfilled a reasonable duty of care commensurate with its business scale and degree of professionalism, thereby presuming that the Jianglin Cosmetics Store actually did not know and should not have known that the product it sold was infringing, and that it had no fault subjectively. Furthermore, the Jianglin Cosmetics Store also provided copies of evidence, including invoices showing Zhongzhuang Company obtaining Nayi Qier Aloe Vera Gel from its upstream merchant Guanmei Company, and import customs declaration forms, entry inspection and quarantine certificates, and special import duty payment books showing Guanmei Company obtaining Nayi Qier Aloe Vera Gel from its upstream merchant Yipinzhuang Company. Although the establishment of the Jianglin Cosmetics Store's legal source defense does not require it to prove that the accused infringing product it sold originated from the rights holder, as a seller, providing copies of the above evidence to the people's court without holding the originals is helpful for the rights holder Nayi Qier to trace the source of the infringement, and also serves as a reference for this Court in reviewing the subjective element. Therefore, the proactive act of adducing evidence by the Jianglin Cosmetics Store to the people's court should be encouraged and affirmed.

In summary, the Jianglin Cosmetics Store has fulfilled its burden of proof regarding the legal source of the accused infringing product and that it has exercised reasonable care. Its legal source defense is established. Pursuant to Article 64, paragraph 2 of the Trademark Law, the Jianglin Cosmetics Store shall not bear liability for damages. The corresponding retrial application grounds of the Jianglin Cosmetics Store are well-founded, and this Court supports them according to law. The determination in the judgment of second instance that the relevant evidence provided by the Jianglin Cosmetics Store could not prove that the goods from its upstream merchant originated from Nayi Qier, nor could it prove that it had authorization from Nayi Qier, and therefore the legal source defense could not be established, was erroneous, and this Court corrects it.

It should be pointed out that the premise for applying the legal source defense system is that the act of selling the accused infringing product constitutes infringement. Therefore, even if the legal source defense is established, it does not change the infringing nature of the act itself. The Trademark Law establishes the legal source defense system to encourage good-faith sellers to disclose product source information by exempting them from liability for damages, thereby promoting the crackdown on the source of infringement. Hence, the establishment of the legal source defense does not require the seller to prove that the product originates from the rights holder; in other words, if the seller can prove that the product it sold originates from the rights holder, then its sales act does not constitute infringement. This situation contradicts the legal spirit of the legal source defense system, i.e., there is no need to consider whether the legal source defense system applies. Where the legal source defense is established, although a good-faith seller is not liable for infringement damages according to law, it must still bear other corresponding infringement liabilities in accordance with legal provisions.

3. Regarding the issue of the Jianglin Cosmetics Store's responsibility. According to Article 179 of the Civil Code of the People's Republic of China, the main methods of bearing civil liability include cessation of infringement, removal of obstacles, and compensation for losses. This Court holds that because the act of the Jianglin Cosmetics Store in selling the accused infringing product infringed on the exclusive right to use the trademark in question of Nayi Qier, it shall bear the civil liability of ceasing the infringement. Nayi Qier also claimed that the Jianglin Cosmetics Store should bear the responsibility for compensating relevant economic losses and paying rights enforcement expenses, specifically RMB 30,000 for economic losses, and rights enforcement expenses of RMB 2,000 for investigation, evidence collection, and notarization fees, and RMB 8,000 for agency fees. This Court holds that rights enforcement expenses are costs incurred by the rights holder to stop the infringement, which are independent from the economic losses suffered due to the infringement, and their legal nature differs from that of damages for infringement. Even if the legal source defense of the Jianglin Cosmetics Store is established in this case, and it is not liable for damages under Article 64 of the Trademark Law, in principle, it should still bear liability for compensating the rights holder's reasonable expenses incurred to obtain relief by way of cessation of infringement.

However, in this case, whether the litigation claim of Nayi Qier regarding rights enforcement expenses should be upheld must be determined comprehensively in light of the specific circumstances of the case and by reverting to the legislative intent of the legal source defense system. First, although Nayi Qier raised the litigation claim that the Jianglin Cosmetics Store should compensate it for rights enforcement expenses, it never provided relevant evidence to the people's court, so it should bear the adverse legal consequences. Second, the provision of the legal source defense system exempting good-faith sellers from liability for damages is, on the one hand, intended to encourage good-faith sellers to proactively disclose product source information, and on the other hand, to protect the reliance interests of good-faith sellers arising from normal market transaction order. In this case, the purchase price and selling price of the accused infringing product were low, the infringement circumstances and consequences were relatively minor, and the Jianglin Cosmetics Store had already identified the provider of the accused infringing product, providing favorable leads for Nayi Qier to trace the source of the infringement. It had fulfilled its reasonable duty of care and was not subjectively at fault. Under these circumstances, if the Jianglin Cosmetics Store were still required to bear such rights enforcement expenses, it would not only violate the principle of fairness but also fail to adequately reflect the incentive and protection of the legal source defense system for good-faith sellers. Third, according to data from the China Judgments Online website, Nayi Qier, based on the same infringing product as in this case, has filed lawsuits against a large number of small and medium-sized sellers in more than ten provinces and regions in mainland China, indicating a situation of batch rights enforcement. Given that in batch litigation cases, rights holders may have common reasonable expenses for stopping the infringement, to prevent the compensation for rights enforcement expenses from exceeding the actual expenses incurred by the rights holder, thereby causing the rights holder to obtain multiple benefits, the reasonableness of the litigation claims should be assessed when determining individual case rights enforcement expenses. Since Nayi Qier failed to provide corresponding evidence of its rights enforcement expenses in this case, this Court cannot separately calculate its rights enforcement expenses in this case, and its corresponding litigation claims lack a basis. In summary, to reflect the incentive and protection of the legal source defense system for good-faith sellers, and to guide intellectual property rights holders to actively assert rights against the producers at the source of infringement, and to enforce rights lawfully and reasonably, this Court does not uphold the litigation claims of Nayi Qier regarding rights enforcement expenses.

It should be made clear here that civil subjects, as holders of intellectual property rights, have the right to lawfully and reasonably protect their own rights and interests. However, the purpose of intellectual property protection is to advocate and encourage the use of creative intellectual achievements, and to transform intangible knowledge wealth into tangible material wealth, thereby promoting the development of productive forces. If "rights enforcement" of intellectual property is used as a means and tool to earn profits, and "litigation" is used as a way to make profits, this not only fails to conform to the purpose of intellectual property protection, but also is detrimental to maintaining the stability of market transaction order, and to a certain extent, wastes judicial resources. Such conduct should not be encouraged or promoted.

(B) Regarding whether the court of second instance's failure to add relevant parties to participate in the lawsuit and its adjudication of related substantive issues violated procedural rules or harmed the rights of the parties.

Upon review, the upstream merchants of the Jianglin Cosmetics Store, Zhongzhuang Company, Guanmei Company, and Yipinzhuang Company, are not necessary co-defendants in this case. The court of second instance's refusal to grant the Jianglin Cosmetics Store's request to add the above parties was not improper. Furthermore, during the trial, the court of second instance's review of whether the Jianglin Cosmetics Store had fulfilled its reasonable duty of care was likewise aimed at ascertaining the key issue of whether the Jianglin Cosmetics Store's legal source defense could be established. There was no circumstance of harming the litigant rights of the parties. The corresponding retrial application grounds of the Jianglin Cosmetics Store cannot be established, and this Court does not support them.

In conclusion, some of the retrial application grounds of the Jianglin Cosmetics Store are established, and this Court supports them. The remaining retrial application grounds are rejected. The judgment of second instance contained errors in both the finding of facts and the application of law, and this Court corrects them. Pursuant to Article 179 of the Civil Code of the People's Republic of China, Articles 57 and 64, paragraph 2 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 4 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Actions Involving Intellectual Property Rights, and Article 177, paragraph 1, subparagraph 2 and Article 214, paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

1. The civil judgment (2021) Ji Zhi Min Zhong Zi No. 26 of the Hebei High People's Court is vacated;

2. The civil judgment (2020) Ji 06 Zhi Min Chu Zi No. 201 of the Baoding Intermediate People's Court, Hebei Province, is vacated;

3. The Wangdu County Jianglin Cosmetics Store shall immediately cease the act of infringing on the exclusive right to use the registered trademark of Nayi Qier Co., Ltd. upon the effective date of this judgment, i.e., cease selling products that infringe on Nayi Qier Co., Ltd.'s exclusive right to use the registered trademark, and destroy the infringing products in stock;

4. All other claims of Nayi Qier Co., Ltd. are rejected.

The first-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 800 shall be borne by Nayi Qier Co., Ltd. in the amount of RMB 600, and by Wangdu County Jianglin Cosmetics Store in the amount of RMB 200. The second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 50 shall be borne by Nayi Qier Co., Ltd.

This judgment is final.
